You write in the formal register at B2 level: you nominalise verbs (tras el cierre, la colocación), organise the text with connectors (en primer lugar, asimismo, cabe destacar, en lo que respecta a, no obstante, por consiguiente) and draft an official letter with the right formulas.
I am writing to request a plaque.
After the bookshop closed, the premises were left empty.
The cultural importance of the place deserves to be stressed.
As regards the costs, we will take care of them.
I look forward to your reply.
To turn verbs into nouns (cerrar → el cierre, colocar → la colocación) to give the text a formal tone.
To order arguments with connectors: en primer lugar, en segundo lugar, por último.
To add and highlight information: asimismo, además, cabe destacar que, conviene subrayar que.
To introduce the topic and the consequence: en lo que respecta a, en cuanto a, por consiguiente, no obstante.
To write a complete official letter: salutation, reason, arguments, closing formula.

31 May, afternoon, calle de las Huertas. Where the La Lámpara bookshop used to be, there is now a small café. The owner, Lola, wants a plaque on the façade. Marta and Ecaterina help her write the application to the city council.
Look, I’ve already written the letter: “Hi, we want to put up a plaque because Señor Andrés is really nice and the bookshop was awesome.”
(laughing) Lola, you don’t say “hi” to the city council. Or “awesome”. Let’s start again: “Dear Sirs:”.
And then? I write novels, but official letters scare me.
Then the reason: “We are writing to you to request the installation of a commemorative plaque.”
“The installation”? Why not “to put up a plaque”?
Because the formal register prefers nouns. You don’t say “because it closed in 1994”, but “following its closure in 1994”.
OK. And then the arguments, right? First of all, the history of the bookshop.
Exactly. Secondly, the novel. Likewise, the impact of the launch at the fair deserves to be stressed.
And the bit about me paying for the plaque? I’ll put that at the end: “I’ll pay for the plaque, don’t worry.”
Almost. “As regards the costs, these will be borne by the owner of the premises.” And to finish: “We look forward to your reply. Yours faithfully.”
Goodness. With this letter they’ll give me the plaque and a medal.
“nos dirigimos” = we are writing to, we address
“correrán a cargo de” = will be borne by
The stress falls on the last syllable: co-lo-ca-CIÓN, re-per-cu-SIÓN, so-li-ci-TUD. They are frequent in formal texts, so practise the rhythm: the syllables before are short and even.
When you read a formal text aloud, make a short pause after a connector at the start: «Asimismo, | cabe destacar…», «No obstante, | la propuesta…». The pause matches the comma.
They have two stresses: one from the adjective and one on “-MEN-”: a-TEN-ta-MEN-te, sin-CE-ra-MEN-te.
In the formal register, many verbs turn into nouns. The text becomes more impersonal and more “official”:
Tras el cierre de la librería…
La publicación de la foto provocó…
Solicitamos la colocación de una placa.
Debido a la decisión de la comisión…
When the bookshop closed in 1994, the premises were left empty. → Following the closure of the bookshop in 1994, the premises were left empty.
Don’t overdo it: too many nouns in a row make the text hard to read («la realización de la revisión de la solicitud» ✗). One or two nominalisations per sentence are enough.
en primer lugar, en segundo lugar, por último
cabe destacar que, conviene subrayar que
en lo que respecta a, en cuanto a, por lo que se refiere a
por consiguiente, por lo tanto, de ahí que (+ subj.)
en definitiva, en resumen, en conclusión
At the start of a sentence, a connector is followed by a comma: «No obstante, la propuesta tiene un inconveniente.» “Cabe destacar que” and “conviene subrayar que” take no comma before “que”.
Me dirijo a usted con el fin de…
dado que… / puesto que… / debido a…
Be consistent with “usted”: «le escribo», «su respuesta», «le agradecería». The common mistake is mixing: «Le escribo para pedirte…» ✗.
4. The structure of an official letter
By means of this letter, we are writing to you in order to…
With nothing further to add, we look forward to your reply.
In Spanish, the salutation is followed by a COLON, not a comma: «Estimada señora:». The next word starts with a capital letter, on the following line.
The correct opening for an official letter
¿Qué quiere poner Lola en la fachada?
¿Por qué no se puede escribir «hola» al Ayuntamiento?
¿Qué se prefiere en el registro formal, según Ecaterina?
The final letter sent to Madrid City Council. Notice the nominalisations and the connectors.

Dear Sirs, by means of this letter we are writing to you to request the installation of a commemorative plaque on the façade of the premises once occupied by the former La Lámpara bookshop, on calle de las Huertas.
First of all, the historical importance of the establishment deserves to be stressed. For decades, the bookshop was a meeting point for readers, writers and translators, both Spanish and foreign.

Secondly, the recent publication of a novel inspired by the life of its bookseller, as well as its translation into Romanian, has aroused great interest. Likewise, the launch held at the Book Fair brought together more than three hundred people.

As regards the costs, these will be borne by the current owner of the premises. With nothing further to add, we look forward to your reply. Yours faithfully, Lola Martín, Marta Gil and Ecaterina Ionescu.
“por medio de la presente” = by means of this letter
“sin otro particular” = with nothing further to add
La colocación de una placa conmemorativa
Un permiso para abrir una librería

On the morning of 31 May, Juan came back from the kiosk in the plaza de Lavapiés with three newspapers under his arm, out of breath, as if he had been running. Andrei’s photo took up half a page of the culture section: Andrés greeting the audience with his hand raised and, behind him, Costel crying with Rosa Elena in his arms. The headline read: “The bookseller who waited forty years”. Juan put the newspapers down on the breakfast table without saying a word, which in his case was the greatest possible sign of emotion.

Andrei called his father in Bucharest to tell him. Señor Dan, who was an engineer and trusted nothing he couldn’t measure, asked him first what the newspaper’s print run was, then how many columns the photo took up and, finally, whether it was in focus. When Andrei confessed it was one of the few that hadn’t come out blurred, his father was silent for a moment and told him he was proud of him. Andrei had to go out onto the balcony so that nobody would see him.

Ecaterina read the article aloud, her glasses on the tip of her nose and the newspaper almost touching her face, because of her cataracts. At every sentence she laughed a little. “The emotion of the reunion deserves to be stressed,” she read. “It is worth highlighting the impact of the event.” She explained to Ana that journalists have a curious habit: they turn tears into nouns. Nobody cried in the article; there was “emotion”. Nobody hugged; there was a “reunion”. She said it was the same language she had translated for ten years at the trade office, and that she was fond of it, even though it was no good for telling anything true.

Before midday, Marta had already received eleven interview requests: three radio stations, two TV channels, several magazines and even a cookery programme that, for reasons nobody understood, wanted to interview Mihai. Ecaterina turned them all down, with a single exception: a young journalist from a local radio station who had written a polite letter, with no mistakes and without the word “viral”. Ecaterina said her story wasn’t a product, and that the novel already told it better than she could.

In the afternoon, when the heat had eased a little, Marta and Ecaterina walked to calle de las Huertas. Ecaterina hadn’t been back there since 1987. In December, on her first visit, she hadn’t dared. Now she walked slowly, leaning on her stick and on Marta’s arm, counting the doorways under her breath, as if she feared the street might have moved. In front of a green wooden door, she stopped. The sign was no longer there, because it now hung in the hallway of the flat on the calle del Prado, but she knew this was the place.

Where the bookshop used to be, there was now a small café with shelves full of second-hand books. It was called “El Mostrador” (The Counter). The owner, a woman of about thirty-five called Lola, was cleaning the coffee machine when she saw them come in. She recognised them at once, from the newspaper. She put down the cloth, took off her apron and told them, very seriously, that she had been waiting seven years for someone from the bookshop to walk through that door.

She told them that when she bought the premises, she found in the basement a cardboard box with old invoices, a pair of rusty scissors and a pile of paper bookmarks with a drawing of a lamp and the words “Librería La Lámpara, Huertas”. She had used some of them to decorate the shelves and kept the rest in a drawer, in case the owner turned up one day. She opened the drawer and gave one to Ecaterina. Ecaterina recognised it instantly: she had designed it herself, in 1983, on a napkin, one rainy afternoon.

Ecaterina sat down at the table at the back, by the window, and began pointing with her stick. There, on the left, was poetry. On the right, history and maps. In the middle, the dark wooden counter where Andrés wrapped books in brown paper. And at the back, exactly where the coffee machine now stood, the old gas heater beside which they had listened to the radio all through the night of 23 February 1981. Lola listened without moving, her mouth slightly open.

It was Lola who had the idea of the plaque. She said that in Madrid there were plaques on the façades of houses where writers had lived, and she didn’t see why there couldn’t be one for a bookseller. Marta explained that it had to be requested from the city council, in writing, with a formal application. Lola burst out laughing. She said she knew how to make coffee, carrot cake and the accounts at the end of the month, but official letters scared her more than the tax office. Ecaterina smiled and said she had spent ten years translating official letters, and that at last they were going to be good for something.

They wrote the letter right there, first on a napkin and then on Marta’s laptop. Lola’s first draft began with “Hi” and ended with “big kiss”. Ecaterina corrected it sentence by sentence, with a teacher’s patience. She explained that in an official letter you don’t write “because the bookshop closed”, but “following the closure of the bookshop”; not “we want you to put it up”, but “we request its installation”. Lola protested that this made it sound as if nobody did anything. Ecaterina replied that that was exactly the point: in official language, things happen by themselves.

That night, in the flat on the calle del Prado, Marta told her grandfather about the plaque. Andrés had slept almost all day; the fair had left him exhausted, as if he had reopened the bookshop single-handed. He listened with his eyes half closed. Then he said plaques were for the dead. Marta froze. But Andrés added, with the ghost of a smile, that in his case the city council would have to wait a little, because he hadn’t finished reading yet.

On 1 June, at seven in the morning, Costel and Andrei left with the lorry. Costel’s boss had found him a load of olive oil for Bucharest, so the return journey wouldn’t be empty. Before they left, Andrés asked to see “the lorry driver”. Costel came into the living room with his cap in his hand, like someone entering a church. Andrés gave him an old road atlas of Spain, from 1980, with the bookshop’s stamp on the first page. “So you don’t get lost,” he told him. Costel couldn’t manage to answer.

The way back went through Valencia. Costel had told his daughter he would stop for lunch with her. His daughter, who knew her father well, had set him a single condition: he could cry in the lorry, on the motorway and in the car park, but not at the table, in front of the neighbours. Andrei said afterwards that Costel kept to the condition for exactly twenty minutes, until his daughter opened the signed copy he had brought her and read what Ecaterina had written.

On 2 June, Pilar had to go back to Seville, because the hospital was expecting her. Before going to the station, she had breakfast with Ecaterina in a café in the plaza de Santa Ana. At first they said little. Then Pilar told her something she had never told anyone: on the worst days of the illness, when her father no longer recognised anyone, he would sometimes sit staring at the green sign in the hallway and call it “E.’s light”. For years, Pilar hadn’t known who E. was. Now she knew.

As they said goodbye at the entrance to Atocha station, Pilar invited her to Seville in the autumn, once she had recovered from the operation. She promised to show her the hospital, the house where she lived and a courtyard with orange trees where, according to her, reading was better than anywhere else in the world. Ecaterina accepted. Then Pilar got on the train and waved goodbye, just like her father at the fair: with a small, elegant, slightly old-fashioned gesture.

That same afternoon, Rosa Elena gave Andrés the drawing of the book lorry, the one she hadn’t wanted to put in the suitcase. Andrés looked at it for a long time. He asked her who the lady sitting next to the driver was. Rosa Elena explained that it was Ecaterina, but younger, because in drawings nobody has cataracts. Andrés laughed so hard he had to ask for a glass of water. Marta said afterwards that she hadn’t heard him laugh like that for months.

The morning of 3 June was one of the good ones. Andrés woke up lucid, asked for a milky coffee and asked about the date, the weather and Ecaterina. When she arrived, he asked her to read to him from his old copy of Rayuela, his, not hers. Ecaterina opened it at the chapter he had underlined in 1979 and began to read. He listened with his eyes closed. At one word he interrupted her to correct her pronunciation, exactly as he used to forty years before, in the back room of the bookshop. She repeated it obediently, and they both laughed.

Then he asked her about the operation. Ecaterina told him it was on 10 June, in Bucharest, and that the doctor had promised she would see colours as before. Andrés nodded. He told her that then she would have to come back to Madrid to see the plaque with new eyes. Then he asked for the 1987 letter, the one still kept between the pages of the book, and held it against his chest for a while. Ecaterina thought he was going to give it to her. But he put it back in the book and said: “The letter stays with the book. And the book, for now, stays with me.”

On the morning of 4 June, Ecaterina went to say goodbye. Marta left them alone. Ecaterina stood for a moment in the living-room doorway, her handbag in one hand and her stick in the other, not knowing what to say. In 1987 she had left Madrid without saying goodbye to him. It had taken her forty years to regret it completely. Now she had had the words ready since the night before, but none of them would come out.

It was Andrés who spoke first. “Are you leaving?” he asked. She said yes, her plane was at twelve. He looked at her for a long time, with a clarity he hadn’t had for days. Then he said: “At last you’re saying goodbye. It took you forty years.” Ecaterina burst out laughing and crying at the same time, and for once she didn’t try to hide either. She went up to him, kissed him on the forehead and said: “See you soon, Andrés.” He answered: “See you soon. And this time, write.”

At the airport, while they were waiting to board, Ecaterina got a message from Marta with a photo: an email from the city council. It was an automatic reply: “You are hereby informed that your application has been registered under file number 2/417. Following its examination by the relevant committee, you will be notified of the decision adopted.” Marta had added a single comment: “Not one active verb.” Ecaterina read it twice and said it was the loveliest letter she had received in years, because it was written in her favourite language: the language of offices.

On the plane, Ecaterina kept looking out of the window until Madrid disappeared beneath the clouds. In her hand she held the La Lámpara bookmark. Ana asked her if she was sad. Ecaterina took a while to answer. Then she said no, she was tired and felt a little strange, but not sad. And she explained why: it was the first time in her life she had left Madrid having said goodbye. Rosa Elena, asleep with her head on her lap, murmured something in her sleep. Ecaterina stroked her hair and closed her eyes.
“cuántos ejemplares tiraba” = what its print run was
